content: 1. Use a soft cloth or a dry sponge to clean the child’s environment. If necessary, employ a gentle “startle effect” to capture the child’s attention and focus. 2. Select toys that are suitable for the child’s age and condition. For instance, for a younger child, create a soft, short noise using a rattle. For an older child, lightly tap a spoon against a metal pot to produce sound. 3. Follow the child’s lead by mimicking their sounds and gestures. Ensure you have the child’s attention and maintain eye contact. Wait for the child to make a movement or sound, even if it is subtle, such as opening and closing their eyes. Then, respond by exaggerating their movements or sounds in a playful and cheerful manner. Continue this interaction until a responsive “conversation” of sounds and gestures is established. 4. If the child does not respond to this interaction, move on to another activity. 5. Engage the child in play and communication using age-appropriate toys and activities. Refer to counseling cards to select suitable activities. For a sick or lethargic child, begin with simpler activities designed for younger age groups. Present one toy at a time to avoid overwhelming the child. Gradually increase the complexity of the activity, such as sorting items into a bowl or creating a game that involves making noise. Praise the child for their efforts and accomplishments, and adjust the activity if the child loses interest. 6. As the child becomes more active, introduce more challenging play or communication activities. Assist the child in starting the activity and observe their responses. Continue to praise their efforts and show delight in their progress. 7. After completing the session, clean the toys used by the child to prevent the transmission of illness. Instruct participants to wash toys before using them with another child. Inpatient Session: Interacting with a Child 1. Approach the child in their bed, which is marked with colored paper. 2. Gain the child’s attention. 3. Follow the child’s lead by mimicking their sounds and gestures. Observe how the child responds. 4. Play and communicate with the child using age-appropriate toys and activities. 5. Gradually increase the child’s level of activity and introduce new skills. 6. Praise the child for their efforts in learning new activities. Before leaving, involve the caregiver in playing with the child, play a “bye-bye” game, or leave a simple toy for the child to play with. Outpatient Session: Counseling the Caregiver 1. During outpatient sessions, participants counsel caregivers rather than directly interacting with the child. They observe the caregiver-child interaction, ask questions to understand how the caregiver plays and communicates with the child at home, and use checklists and counseling cards to guide the session. 2. Participants coach caregivers to try new activities, helping them recognize the child’s cues and respond appropriately. On Day 3, participants also assist caregivers in solving problems related to providing care at home. 3. The goal is for participants to work in pairs, seeing three to five children and their caregivers during each session. One participant interviews and counsels the caregiver while the other observes, and both complete a checklist for the session. 4. Facilitators should remind participants to focus on assisting the caregiver rather than directly engaging with the child, as this helps the child bond with the caregiver rather than the counselor. Preparation for Outpatient Sessions 1. 2. Identify spaces where participants can work in pairs to counsel caregivers and their children. 3. Ensure the flow of children and caregivers through the facility is organized, from entry to counseling and back to receiving treatments or services. 4. Prepare materials, including toys, and ensure they are clean and readily available. 5. Identify caregivers and children willing to participate in a demonstration of a counseling session. Tasks During Outpatient Sessions 1. Introduce the purpose of the session and the activities. Participants will work in pairs, with one counseling the caregiver and the other observing. Both should complete a checklist for the child. 2. Facilitators will observe and provide feedback to help participants improve their counseling skills. 3. During the first session, participants practice greeting caregivers and children, asking questions, observing interactions, praising caregivers, and advising them. They use checklists and counseling cards to guide the process. 4. On Day 3, participants help caregivers solve problems related to care at home. Demonstration of Counseling Session 1. Greet the caregiver warmly and interview them to complete the top section of the checklist. 2. Observe the caregiver-child interaction, noting how the caregiver responds to the child’s movements, comforts the child, and shows affection. 3. Ask questions to understand how the caregiver plays and communicates with the child and their perception of the child’s development. 4. Praise the caregiver for specific positive actions they are doing for the child. 5. Advise the caregiver on play and communication activities to do at home, helping them recognize the child’s cues and respond appropriately. Explain how these activities will support the child’s growth and learning. 6. Check the caregiver’s understanding by observing them try the activity and providing guidance as needed. 7. On Day 3, discuss any challenges the caregiver faces in playing and communicating with the child at home and help them find solutions. Debriefing and Review 1. After the caregiver and child leave, review the counseling session with participants. Discuss the steps taken, the activities selected, and the caregiver and child’s responses. 2. Ask participants how the session could be improved. On Day 3, encourage participants to observe and reflect on the caregiver-child interaction. 3. Use photos or videos taken during the session to illustrate good examples of counseling skills. 4. Discuss which activities were most appropriate for the children and why.
